frameworks.name: Erikson’s Psychosocial Stages
frameworks.author: Erik H. Erikson
frameworks.summary: Eight life stages, each with its own challenge and strength.
frameworks.about: A classic developmental model: across life we meet a series of social and emotional turning points.
frameworks.scope: Thinking about growth across a lifetime.
frameworks.limits: A broad theory, not a test. Ages are approximate and cultures differ. Never use it to diagnose anyone.
frameworks.notice: Summaries and My-first wording are Minest’s own. Concept names are standard terms; no protected text is copied.

frameworks.name: Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs
frameworks.author: Abraham Maslow
frameworks.summary: From basic needs to growth: what people need to live and to flourish.
frameworks.about: Often drawn as a pyramid (a later illustration). Maslow saw needs as overlapping, not strict steps.
frameworks.scope: Reflecting on what helps you and others thrive.
frameworks.limits: Research supports the needs but not a fixed order. Not a diagnostic tool.
frameworks.notice: Summaries and My-first wording are Minest’s own. Concept names are standard terms; no protected text is copied.

frameworks.name: Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy
frameworks.author: L. W. Anderson & D. R. Krathwohl (after B. S. Bloom)
frameworks.summary: Six kinds of thinking, from remembering to creating.

concepts.name: Understand
concepts.summary: Explain ideas in your own words.

concepts.name: Apply
concepts.summary: Use what you know in a new situation.

concepts.name: Analyze
concepts.summary: Break it into parts and see how they relate.

concepts.name: Create
concepts.summary: Put things together into something new.

source.work: A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing

frameworks.about: The 2001 revision of Bloom’s 1956 taxonomy uses verbs and adds a knowledge dimension (factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive).
frameworks.limits: Levels overlap in real learning; it is a planning aid, not a ranking of students.
frameworks.notice: Summaries and My-first wording are Minest’s own. Concept names are standard terms; no protected text is copied.

frameworks.name: Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory
frameworks.author: Urie Bronfenbrenner
frameworks.summary: A person grows inside layers of surroundings, from family to culture to time.

concepts.name: Individual
concepts.summary: The person at the centre — age, health, temperament.

concepts.name: Microsystem
concepts.summary: Settings you take part in directly: family, school, friends, neighbourhood.

concepts.name: Mesosystem
concepts.summary: Links between those settings — e.g. family and school working together.

concepts.name: Exosystem
concepts.myName: What affects me from a distance
concepts.summary: Settings you are not in that still affect you — a parent’s workplace, local services.

concepts.name: Macrosystem
concepts.summary: Culture, values, laws, economy and beliefs that shape everything inside.

concepts.name: Chronosystem
concepts.summary: Change over time — life transitions and historical events.

frameworks.about: Bronfenbrenner described development as shaped by nested systems. He later added the person’s own characteristics and processes (the bioecological model).
frameworks.scope: Seeing the circles of people, places and forces around a life.
frameworks.limits: A way to describe influences, not to judge a person or family. Never a diagnosis.
frameworks.notice: Summaries and My-first wording are Minest’s own. Concept names are standard terms; no protected text is copied.
